messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai had always been a rock for his family, but when his young daughter was diagnosed with leukemia, he felt the ground beneath him give way. The months that followed were a blur of hospital visits, medical procedures, and sleepless nights spent worrying about her prognosis. He remembered the sound of her labored breathing, the tubes snaking out of her small body, and the antiseptic smell that clung to everything. Those memories still haunted him, even years after she had passed away. Whenever Kai saw someone from the hospital or caught a glimpse of an ambulance on the street, he felt a familiar tightness in his chest. He would try to shake off the feeling, telling himself it was just anxiety, but deep down, he knew it was more than that. When he started experiencing difficulty breathing or felt short of breath, it was like his body was reliving those terrible moments all over again. These physical sensations triggered a cascade of thoughts: "Something bad is happening," "I'm losing control," and "I'll never be able to protect the people I love." The fear that gripped him in those moments was suffocating. Kai tried to avoid anything that might remind him of those traumatic days – hospitals, medical examinations, even certain TV shows or movies. He threw himself into his work as a project manager, using his tasks and deadlines as a mental distraction from the dark thoughts that lurked beneath the surface. But no matter how hard he worked, he couldn't shake off the feeling of self-blame that had settled in after his daughter's passing. "If only I had been more vigilant," he would think, "maybe she wouldn't have gotten so sick." This self-doubt seeped into other areas of his life, making him question every decision, no matter how small. As Kai navigated his daily routine, he found himself constantly on the lookout for potential threats. When a project was delayed or someone didn't respond to an email right away, he would assume the worst: "Something's gone wrong," or "They're hiding something from me." His body would react with a surge of adrenaline, leaving him feeling jittery and on edge. He knew this wasn't rational, but he couldn't seem to calm his mind. Kai's attempts to suppress these thoughts only seemed to make them stronger. The more he tried to distract himself, the more his mind wandered back to those terrible memories. He felt like he was trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear and self-doubt. And yet, despite all this, Kai couldn't help but feel a deep-seated sense of responsibility for what had happened to his daughter. "I should have protected her," he would think, the guilt and shame washing over him like a wave. As the months turned into years, Kai's relationships with friends and family began to suffer. He became withdrawn, unable to connect with others or enjoy activities that used to bring him joy. His work performance began to slip, too, as his preoccupation with potential threats and his own perceived shortcomings consumed more and more of his mental energy. It was only when he realized he couldn't go on living like this – constantly on edge, forever trapped in the past – that Kai knew he needed help. He hoped therapy could teach him how to break free from this cycle of fear and self-blame, but deep down, he wondered if it was already too late.
